_doc: Lanes for the Organization Timelines tab (build_viewer.py -> timeline_data.py). Each lane: label shown; cat (aid|edu|rights|vig); orgs = database organization names whose members feed the lane; kw = regex searched in Julie Winch's notes, taking the year written right after the society's name (e.g. 'Member, Daughters of Absalom (1827)'); pas = row number in pas1838_beneficial.json (founding year and 1837 figures); pasNote = why a match is only probable. Rows of the 1838 PAS table not listed here are added automatically as lanes of their own. marks = [year, text] for a dated fact with no named people (drawn as a hollow dot).

lanes.label: Friendly Society
marks: Established 1796; 85 members in 1813 (Arthur Donaldson, Juvenile Magazine, July 1813). The 1838 report gives 1795.

lanes.label: Philadelphia African Lodge (Masons)
marks: 'African Lodge, No. 459, established June 24, 1809', '514 members' as printed (Arthur Donaldson, Juvenile Magazine, July 1813). The magazine's total of 590 for all the societies works only if the figure was 154.

lanes.label: Angolian Society
marks: 'The Angola Society': established November 1808; 26 members in 1813 (Arthur Donaldson, Juvenile Magazine, July 1813).

lanes.label: Sons of Africa
marks: Established March 6, 1810; 49 members in 1813 (Arthur Donaldson, Juvenile Magazine, July 1813).

lanes.label: Benezet Society (Benezet Philanthropic)
lanes.pasNote: Probably the society Winch records as the Benezet Philanthropic; the 1838 report gives no founding year.
marks: The Benezette Philanthropic Society: established June 18, 1812; 52 members in 1813 (Arthur Donaldson, Juvenile Magazine, July 1813).

lanes.label: African Friendly Society of St. Thomas
Female Benevolent Society of St. Thomas
marks: 'The Female Benevolent Society': established November 3, 1803; 95 members in 1813 (Arthur Donaldson, Juvenile Magazine, July 1813). Probably this society.

lanes.label: African Benevolent Association (Male African Benevolent Society)
lanes.pasNote: The 1838 report's 'Male African Benevolent Society, instituted 1819' is probably Winch's African Benevolent Association, whose officers she dates to 1819.

lanes.label: Friendly Sons of Zion
lanes.kw: Friendly Benevolent Sons of Zion|Friendly Sons of Zion
lanes.pasNote: Probably the society Winch records as the Society of the Friendly Benevolent Sons of Zion.

lanes.label: African Porter Benevolent Society
marks: Gave to the Vigilance Committee's fund for the Christiana prisoners (Frederick Douglass' Paper, Mar. 4, 1852): 'Porters' Beneficial', $5

lanes.label: Sons of St. Thomas
marks: Established February 15, 1812; 28 members in 1813 (Arthur Donaldson, Juvenile Magazine, July 1813). The 1838 report gives 1829, so it may have been re-formed.

lanes.label: Daughters of Ethiopia
marks: Female Society, the Daughters of Ethiopia: established January 8, 1811; 30 members in 1813 (Arthur Donaldson, Juvenile Magazine, July 1813).

lanes.label: African Farmers and Mechanics Society
marks: 'Farmers and Mechanics': established January 18, 1812; about 36 members in 1813 (Arthur Donaldson, Juvenile Magazine, July 1813).

lanes.label: Harrison Benevolent Society
lanes.pasNote: Matched to the report's 'Male Harrison Benevolent Society'.

lanes.label: Daughters of Clayton Durham
marks: Gave to the Vigilance Committee's fund for the Christiana prisoners (Frederick Douglass' Paper, Mar. 4, 1852): $10

lanes.label: United Daughters of St. Mark
marks: Gave to the Vigilance Committee's fund for the Christiana prisoners (Frederick Douglass' Paper, Mar. 4, 1852): $5

lanes.label: Female Granville Society
lanes.pasNote: The 1838 report says instituted 1833, but Winch lists members in 1826.

orgs: Agricultural and Mechanics Association of Pennsylvania and New Jersey

lanes.label: Daughters of Temperance, Hope Grand Union
orgs: Hope Grand Union, Daughters of Temperance
marks: Gave to the Vigilance Committee's fund for the Christiana prisoners (Frederick Douglass' Paper, Mar. 4, 1852): 'Grand Union Daughters of Temperance', $2.50

lanes.label: Grand United Order of Love and Charity
orgs: Grand Tabernacle of Pennsylvania, Grand United Order of Brothers and Sisters of Love and Charity
Grand United Order of Brothers and Sisters of Love and Charity

lanes.label: Daughters of Samaria
marks: Female Society, the Daughters of Samaria: established June 10, 1812; 24 members in 1813 (Arthur Donaldson, Juvenile Magazine, July 1813).

lanes.label: St. James's Society
marks: Established February 14, 1812; 11 members in 1813 (Arthur Donaldson, Juvenile Magazine, July 1813).

lanes.label: Willing's Alley school (Friends, 1771)
marks: Established 1771, free, under the care of the Monthly Meetings of Friends (Arthur Donaldson, Juvenile Magazine, July 1813).
October 26, 1811: 50 boys and 54 girls, plus a free night school of about 60 run by an association of young men (Donaldson's count).
May 12, 1813: 48 boys taught by Zebulon Holmes and 48 girls taught by Mary Walton (Donaldson's count).
Part free and part pay: boys 72 on the roll, 45 attending; girls 82 on the roll, 40 attending (Abolition Society report, 1838).

lanes.label: Ruth Hand's school, Race Street (Bray's, Episcopal fund, c. 1786)
marks: Established about 1786; reading and sewing, supported by a fund belonging to the Episcopal Church under three trustees (Arthur Donaldson, Juvenile Magazine, July 1813).
May 12, 1813: 7 boys and 29 girls (Donaldson's count).

'Bray's' free school: 12 on the roll, 10 attending (Abolition Society report, 1838). Julie Winch notes that Ruth Hand was mistress of this girls' school, supported by the Associates of Dr. Bray, in 1824.

lanes.label: Jane Hut's school, Sixth Street (1803)
marks: Established 1803 (Arthur Donaldson, Juvenile Magazine, July 1813).
May 12, 1813: 9 boys and 13 girls, taught by Jane Hut (Donaldson's count).

lanes.label: Quomony Clarkson's school, Green's Court (1804)
marks: Established 1804, in Green's Court between Spruce and Pine (Arthur Donaldson, Juvenile Magazine, July 1813).
October 26, 1811: about 50 boys and girls, and a night school of about 30 (Donaldson's count).
May 12, 1813: 31 boys and 19 girls (Donaldson's count).

lanes.label: Arthur Donaldson's school for children of colour (1809)
orgs: Arthur Donaldson's School for People of Colour
marks: Opened May 1, 1809 in Front Street between Arch and Race, with four scholars.
Schoolroom burned October 23, 1811; reopened five days later at Wood and Crown streets.
May 12, 1813: 55 boys and 52 girls, plus a night school. Arthur Donaldson printed his rolls in The Juvenile Magazine, July 1813.

lanes.label: John Gloucester's school, Seventh below Shippen (1810)
orgs: John Gloucester's school, Seventh below Shippen
marks: Established 1810 (Arthur Donaldson, Juvenile Magazine, July 1813).
May 12, 1813: 16 boys and 11 girls (Donaldson's count).

lanes.label: Union Society for schools and domestic manufactures (1810)
marks: 'The Union Society, for the support of schools and domestic manufactures, for the benefit of the African race and people of colour, established in 1810' (Arthur Donaldson, Juvenile Magazine, July 1813).

lanes.label: Solomon Clarkson's school, Lombard Street (1812)
marks: Established by Solomon Clarkson, October 27, 1812 (Arthur Donaldson, Juvenile Magazine, July 1813).
May 12, 1813: 19 boys and 5 girls (Donaldson's count).
Still teaching: a pay school with 40 on the roll, all 40 attending (Abolition Society report, 1838).

lanes.label: Clarkson School (Abolition Society), Cherry Alley, later Raspberry Street (1813)
marks: Established by the Abolition Society March 1, 1813, free; 52 boys, taught by James Kelly, on May 12, 1813 (Arthur Donaldson, Juvenile Magazine, July 1813).

The Clarkson School: girls 72 on the roll and 40 attending (part free, part pay); boys at Clarkson Hall under G. Luther, 50 on the roll and 45 attending (pay) (Abolition Society report, 1838). The school began in Cherry Alley and later moved to Raspberry Street.

lanes.label: Lombard Street public school (1838 report)
marks: Free public school: boys 200 on the roll, 150 attending; girls 263 on the roll, 160 attending (Abolition Society report, 1838).

lanes.label: Northern Liberties public school (1838 report)
marks: Free public school: 220 on the roll, 84 attending (Abolition Society report, 1838).

lanes.label: Infant schools: Locust Street, Adelphi, Tidmarsh (1838 report)
marks: Free infant schools: Locust Street 120 on the roll, Adelphi 90, Tidmarsh 82 (Abolition Society report, 1838).

lanes.label: Adelphi school, boys (1838 report)
marks: Free school: 88 on the roll, 60 attending (Abolition Society report, 1838).

lanes.label: Shelter for Colored Orphans (1838 report)
marks: Free school: 41 on the roll, all attending (Abolition Society report, 1838).

lanes.label: Pay schools under white teachers (1838 report)
marks: Mount Zion Church, Is. Corbet, 17 on the roll; Elizabeth Street, Abigail Brown, 35 (Abolition Society report, 1838).

lanes.label: Pay schools taught by colored teachers (1838 report)
orgs: Pay schools taught by colored teachers (1838)
marks: Ten schools, 288 on the rolls and 260 attending (Abolition Society report, 1838).

lanes.label: Library Company of Colored Persons
orgs: Philadelphia Library Company of Colored Persons

lanes.label: Committee of Vigilance against kidnapping (1827)
marks: Twenty members appointed at Bethel Church to help catch the kidnappers of Philadelphia children (U.S. Gazette, Feb. 23, 1827)

lanes.label: Protecting Society of the City and County of Philadelphia
orgs: Protecting Society of the City and County of Philadelphia
marks: Formed in 1827, as its notices state
Notices in Freedom's Journal, dated Philadelphia, April 24, 1828; John Allen, secretary

orgs: Committee of Vigilance to support the Rights of All (1829)

marks: Assembled and marched armed through the city; described in Amos Webber's diary and objected to by the Daily Ledger
